title: Scientists Burned Their Own Scrolls to Read Ancient Ones
summary:
What would you do to solve a 2,000-year-old mystery? One scientist burned his own scrolls — on purpose!

Here's the story. In 79 C.E., Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the Roman city of Herculaneum. A library of over 1,000 papyrus scrolls was turned into charred, fragile lumps. They're the only intact library from ancient times. But opening them would turn them to dust.

So Douglas Seiler had an idea. He got papyrus and ink from Egypt and Japan. He paid high school students to write on them with passages from Star Wars and the Bible. Then he burned them. Why? To test if lead in the ink could be seen with X-rays.

It worked! Lead absorbs X-rays up to 25 times better than burned papyrus. So writing with lead ink shows up clearly on X-ray CT scans. A cheap handheld scanner can even find lead in a scroll without opening it.

This could help researchers read the Herculaneum scrolls virtually. "The value in this project is practically unquantifiable," said one expert. These scrolls might contain lost works of ancient philosophy. Talk about a hot read!
why_it_matters: It shows that a clever experiment — even one that starts with burning your own work — can solve a puzzle that seemed impossible, like reading a book without ever opening it.

background_read: Mount Vesuvius (a volcano in Italy) erupted in 79 C.E. and buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and rock.
Papyrus (a paper made from a plant that grows beside the Nile River in Egypt) was what ancient Egyptians and Romans wrote on, long before paper as we know it was invented.

The library found at Herculaneum is the only complete library left from ancient times. Today scientists use X-ray machines — the same kind doctors use to look at bones — to see inside the scrolls without opening them.
Article_Structure: WHO: Douglas Seiler, the scientist who burned his own scrolls on purpose, with help from high school students who copied out texts.
WHAT: A test showing that lead in old ink shows up clearly on X-ray scans, so burned scrolls can be read without being opened.
WHERE: The ancient scrolls come from Herculaneum, a Roman city buried by Mount Vesuvius in Italy; the papyrus and ink for the test came from Egypt and Japan.
WHY: Researchers hope to read the lost books from the Herculaneum library, which opening by hand would turn to dust.

perspectives.description: They are thrilled, because the scrolls may hold lost works of ancient philosophy that no one has read for 2,000 years.
They worry that scanning cannot show everything, and that the fragile scrolls could still be harmed if people handle them too much.
They point out that the trick worked because of lead in the ink, so scrolls written with different inks may be much harder to read.
